qs.q: A patient presents with symptoms of ulnar nerve entrapment. Which of the following is a recognized site of compression for the ulnar nerve along its course?
qs.e: The ulnar nerve can be entrapped at the cubital tunnel located behind the medial epicondyle between the two heads of the flexor carpi ulnaris. The carpal tunnel is the primary site for median nerve compression.
qs.s: SDL Revision Mock Marathon — Upper Limb, Histology & Embryology —: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with an apical lung mass, Horner syndrome, and ulnar nerve pain. What is the diagnosis?
o: Pancoast (superior sulcus) tumour at the lung apex.
Superior vena cava obstruction causing facial swelling.
qs.e: Pancoast tumors occur at the lung apex and invade the sympathetic chain (Horner syndrome) and the brachial plexus (C8-T2 distribution pain).

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The ulnar nerve supplies motor and sensory function to the medial forearm, hand and fingers. Injury patterns reflect its long course and superficial position at the elbow and wrist.

sections.p: The ulnar nerve is a terminal branch of the medial cord of the brachial plexus (C8‑T1). It travels down the arm, crossing the elbow in the cubital tunnel and the wrist in Guyon's canal.
b: Provides motor to intrinsic hand muscles
Supplies sensation to the medial one‑and‑a‑half digits

sections.p: In the arm it runs medial to the brachial artery, then pierces the medial intermuscular septum. At the elbow it lies posterior to the medial epicondyle within the cubital tunnel.
b: Course: arm → cubital tunnel → forearm → Guyon's canal → hand

sections.p: Close to the brachial artery proximally, the median nerve laterally, and the flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU) which it innervates. At the wrist it lies superficial to the flexor retinaculum.
b: Muscular: FCU and flexor digitorum profundus (ulnar half)

sections.p: The ulnar nerve receives blood from the ulnar recurrent artery proximally and branches of the ulnar artery distally.
b: Ischemia rare but can occur with severe forearm trauma

sections.p: Motor: FCU, medial half of flexor digitorum profundus, most intrinsic hand muscles. Sensory: skin over the medial hand, little finger, and half of the ring finger.
b: Dual innervation of flexor pollicis brevis (median + ulnar)

sections.p: Enables wrist adduction, flexion of the fourth and fifth digits, and fine motor tasks like pinching and typing. Sensory input guides grip force and hand positioning.
b: Protects hand from injury via sensation

sections.p: Compression at the cubital tunnel (cubital tunnel syndrome) or Guyon's canal (ulnar tunnel syndrome) causes sensory loss and intrinsic hand weakness. Trauma can transect the nerve.
b: Symptoms: numbness in little finger, claw hand, weakened grip
Common causes: prolonged elbow flexion, repetitive pressure, fractures, iatrogenic injury

t.b: Confirms demyelination vs axonal loss; guides prognosis
Visualizes nerve swelling or entrapment when EMG unavailable

sections.p: Test sensation with light touch over the little finger and ulnar half of the ring finger. Test motor strength by asking the patient to hold a paper between thumb and little finger (Froment sign).
b: Positive Froment sign suggests ulnar weakness
Weakness of finger abduction points to ulnar neuropathy

whenToSeekHelp: Progressive weakness leading to loss of hand function
Severe pain or swelling after trauma suggesting nerve transection
Signs of infection (redness, fever) over the elbow or wrist

faq.q: Why does a patient develop a claw hand?
faq.a: Loss of ulnar intrinsic muscles unbalances finger extensors, causing hyperextension at MCP joints and flexion at IP joints.

faq.q: Can the ulnar nerve recover after compression?
faq.a: Yes, if decompression occurs before irreversible axonal loss; early physiotherapy improves outcomes.

faq.q: Is the ulnar nerve ever used for grafts?
faq.a: It can be harvested for nerve grafts, but donor site morbidity (hand weakness) must be considered.

exam: Describe the anatomical course of the ulnar nerve from the brachial plexus to the hand.
Explain the clinical signs of ulnar neuropathy at the elbow versus the wrist.
Interpret a nerve conduction study showing slowed conduction velocity across the cubital tunnel.
